consensus_summary: The fixed phrase 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' primarily symbolizes the extreme anguish, despair, and remorse of those condemned and excluded from God's kingdom at eschatological judgment (often under hell's torment); a well-attested alternative reads the gnashing as defiant rage rather than penitential sorrow, drawn from OT and Acts usages, with further minority debates over duration or historical referent.
book_summary: The rage of the wicked at the righteous—what the excluded do at the sight of the kingdom they forfeited, combining sorrow and hatred in one face, after which they melt away; defined via the wicked against the just, staged at Stephen's trial, and templated in the psalm (see, be grieved, gnash, and perish).
consensus_core_identification: extreme anguish/despair/remorse of the condemned at final judgment and exclusion
book_core_identification: rage (with sorrow/hatred) of the wicked/excluded upon seeing the forfeited kingdom, followed by melting away
boundary_disagreement: Book prioritizes rage/hatred ending in melt-away/perishing and roots the idiom in OT/Acts hostility patterns, whereas consensus primary centers ongoing remorseful anguish (commonly under everlasting torment) and treats rage mainly as alternative; book thereby excludes pure-remorse/eternal-torment readings of the same judgment scenes.
material_contradiction: Book's sequence of gnashing then melting away/perishing conflicts with the consensus primary (and the book's own noted common view) of conscious everlasting torment in which the weeping and gnashing occur as continuing misery.
rationale: Minimum cores share the same general referent—the negative reaction of the excluded at the sight of the kingdom/judgment—but the book materially alters precision, emotional register, and aftermath by elevating the common rage alternative, fusing it with sorrow, and appending 'melt away' from Ps 112:10. This preserves category while narrowing and reclassifying boundaries (rejecting pure anguish and eternal-torment settings), yielding REFINED rather than MATCH, DIVERGENT (no full replacement of referent), or NOVEL (rage and perish already appear among listed alternatives).
strongest_objection: The NT judgment refrain consistently pairs gnashing with weeping and images of exclusion/fire/darkness, which the consensus reads as sorrowful anguish under ongoing punishment; OT rage texts and 'melt away' may not control the Matthean/Lukan idiom or overturn traditional eternal-torment associations.
